{
  "hook": "El Reventón comes from a single vineyard at 1,100 meters in the Sierra de Gredos, where 80-year-old Garnacha vines push through decomposed volcanic granite — a geology that shows up in the glass as a smoky, mineral-edged quality you won't find in warmer-climate Garnacha. The addition of Alicante Henri Bouschet, a teinturier grape with pigmented flesh, pushes the color into near-opaque territory while adding tannic grip that lets this wine outlast most Spanish reds at the table.",
  "wine_summary": "Comando G is the project of Daniel Landi and Fernando Garcia, who spent years mapping old-vine Garnacha parcels across the Sierra de Gredos before establishing this domaine in the Cebreros appellation. El Reventón is their village-level bottling — a blend of Garnacha Tinta and the lesser-known Alicante Henri Bouschet from a specific high-altitude plot. The appellation sits at 800 to 1,200 meters elevation, where granitic soils dominate and diurnal temperature swings keep acidity locked in despite the wine's 15% ABV. This isn't a regional generic — it's a site-specific wine that happens to carry a table-wine designation because Cebreros lacks formal DOP status, a technicality that doesn't diminish what's in the bottle.",
  "terroir_expression": "The Sierra de Gredos sits on a batholith of Hercynian granite weathered into sandy, fast-draining soils that force vine roots deep in search of water and minerals. At 1,100 meters, El Reventón experiences continental extremes — summer days reach 35°C, but nights drop to 8°C, preserving malic acid and slowing phenolic development so tannins ripen without fruit fatigue. The volcanic influence shows as a subtle iron-earth character on the palate, distinct from the pure red-fruit expression you'd get from lower-altitude Garnacha. Old vines (80+ years) with fragmented root systems access multiple soil strata, adding savory complexity that younger-vine examples lack.",
  "vinification_summary": "Comando G employs whole-cluster fermentation in open wooden vats, a choice that introduces stem tannins and promotes slow, oxygen-permeable extraction — the stems act as a scaffold controlling maceration pace. Native yeast fermentation follows, allowing indigenous microbial terroir to shape aroma profiles rather than domesticated strains. The blend with Alicante Henri Bouschet is deliberate: the grape's colored pulp (teinturier character) intensifies hue and contributes laevopimaric acid, which stabilizes color against oxidation. Fourteen months in used oak foudres avoids vanilla overwhelming the volcanic-mineral core, letting the granite terroir remain the structural spine.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Suckling pig roasted with rosemary and garlic — the wine's tannic grip cuts through porky collagen fat while the smoky granite note bridges the herb rub",
    "Smoky eggplant dip (baba ganoush) with house-made pita — high altitude Garnacha's earthiness matches the charred vegetable character without overpowering the dish",
    "Castellan-style potatoes with chorizo — the wine's dark fruit and spice echo the pimentón in the sausage while acidity lifts the potato starch",
    "Aged Manchego with quince membrillo — rare pairing, but the wine's mineral austerity stands up to the cheese's salt crystals and contrasts the sweet paste",
    "Venison loin with blackberry reduction — the wine's blackberry core and smoky earthiness align with the sauce; tannin tenderizes the lean protein"
  ],
  "comparable_wines": "Comando G La Viña de la Casa — same producer, higher designation, more concentration and vineyard specificity, but 2x the price for marginal quality gains if you want the terroir story. Marañones Montetra — Garnacha from similar altitude in the Gredos, slightly warmer expression, good alternative if El Reventón is unavailable. Albamar El クエルポ — whole-cluster Garnacha from granite soils, slightly lighter frame but shares the smoky-mineral signature at comparable price.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins, volcanic-mineral backbone, and dark fruit intensity from high-altitude Garnacha and Alicante Bouschet.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "The 2022 vintage has the structure to hold 12 to 15 years in proper cellar conditions (55% humidity, 12-14°C). If drinking now, open 90 minutes before service to allow the reduction to blow off and the mineral character to emerge.",
  "value_assessment": "Current releases sit in the $55 to $70 retail range. At that price, you're competing with Rioja Gran Reserva and Ribera del Duero Pingus-adjacent wines — but El Reventón offers something neither can: volcanic granite terroir and teinturier complexity at this price point is genuinely rare. Worth the money if you want Spain's mineral frontier rather than its traditional signatures.",
  "market_position": "This wine lives on sommelier-driven restaurant lists where adventurous diners seek something different from the California-C Bordeaux paradigm. Retail placement skews toward specialty importers (Jenny & François, Rosenthal) rather than mainstream chains. The collector audience is smaller than Rioja's but growing — Comando G has a 6-to-8-month allocation lag on recent vintages, which tells you demand outpaces supply. Casual drinkers should note: this wine rewards patience and food context; it's not a easy-drinking crowd-pleaser.",
  "insider_take": "Most buyers treat El Reventón as a Garnacha showcase, but the real story is Alicante Henri Bouschet — it's the structural skeleton holding the wine together, adding tannins that let it age like a Cabernet without the varietal cliché. If you dismiss it as a blending grape, you're missing why this wine outlasts most Spanish reds at 10 years old. The table-wine designation trips up collectors who equate appellation status with quality, but Comando G chose this category deliberately to avoid appellation restrictions on blending — the wine is better for it.",

parsed.hook: El Reventón comes from a single vineyard at 1,100 meters in the Sierra de Gredos, where 80-year-old Garnacha vines push through decomposed volcanic granite — a geology that shows up in the glass as a smoky, mineral-edged quality you won't find in warmer-climate Garnacha. The addition of Alicante Henri Bouschet, a teinturier grape with pigmented flesh, pushes the color into near-opaque territory while adding tannic grip that lets this wine outlast most Spanish reds at the table.
parsed.wine_summary: Comando G is the project of Daniel Landi and Fernando Garcia, who spent years mapping old-vine Garnacha parcels across the Sierra de Gredos before establishing this domaine in the Cebreros appellation. El Reventón is their village-level bottling — a blend of Garnacha Tinta and the lesser-known Alicante Henri Bouschet from a specific high-altitude plot. The appellation sits at 800 to 1,200 meters elevation, where granitic soils dominate and diurnal temperature swings keep acidity locked in despite the wine's 15% ABV. This isn't a regional generic — it's a site-specific wine that happens to carry a table-wine designation because Cebreros lacks formal DOP status, a technicality that doesn't diminish what's in the bottle.
parsed.terroir_expression: The Sierra de Gredos sits on a batholith of Hercynian granite weathered into sandy, fast-draining soils that force vine roots deep in search of water and minerals. At 1,100 meters, El Reventón experiences continental extremes — summer days reach 35°C, but nights drop to 8°C, preserving malic acid and slowing phenolic development so tannins ripen without fruit fatigue. The volcanic influence shows as a subtle iron-earth character on the palate, distinct from the pure red-fruit expression you'd get from lower-altitude Garnacha. Old vines (80+ years) with fragmented root systems access multiple soil strata, adding savory complexity that younger-vine examples lack.
parsed.vinification_summary: Comando G employs whole-cluster fermentation in open wooden vats, a choice that introduces stem tannins and promotes slow, oxygen-permeable extraction — the stems act as a scaffold controlling maceration pace. Native yeast fermentation follows, allowing indigenous microbial terroir to shape aroma profiles rather than domesticated strains. The blend with Alicante Henri Bouschet is deliberate: the grape's colored pulp (teinturier character) intensifies hue and contributes laevopimaric acid, which stabilizes color against oxidation. Fourteen months in used oak foudres avoids vanilla overwhelming the volcanic-mineral core, letting the granite terroir remain the structural spine.
food_pairing: Suckling pig roasted with rosemary and garlic — the wine's tannic grip cuts through porky collagen fat while the smoky granite note bridges the herb rub
Smoky eggplant dip (baba ganoush) with house-made pita — high altitude Garnacha's earthiness matches the charred vegetable character without overpowering the dish
Castellan-style potatoes with chorizo — the wine's dark fruit and spice echo the pimentón in the sausage while acidity lifts the potato starch
Aged Manchego with quince membrillo — rare pairing, but the wine's mineral austerity stands up to the cheese's salt crystals and contrasts the sweet paste
Venison loin with blackberry reduction — the wine's blackberry core and smoky earthiness align with the sauce; tannin tenderizes the lean protein
parsed.comparable_wines: Comando G La Viña de la Casa — same producer, higher designation, more concentration and vineyard specificity, but 2x the price for marginal quality gains if you want the terroir story. Marañones Montetra — Garnacha from similar altitude in the Gredos, slightly warmer expression, good alternative if El Reventón is unavailable. Albamar El クエルポ — whole-cluster Garnacha from granite soils, slightly lighter frame but shares the smoky-mineral signature at comparable price.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins, volcanic-mineral backbone, and dark fruit intensity from high-altitude Garnacha and Alicante Bouschet.
parsed.cellar_recommendation: The 2022 vintage has the structure to hold 12 to 15 years in proper cellar conditions (55% humidity, 12-14°C). If drinking now, open 90 minutes before service to allow the reduction to blow off and the mineral character to emerge.
parsed.value_assessment: Current releases sit in the $55 to $70 retail range. At that price, you're competing with Rioja Gran Reserva and Ribera del Duero Pingus-adjacent wines — but El Reventón offers something neither can: volcanic granite terroir and teinturier complexity at this price point is genuinely rare. Worth the money if you want Spain's mineral frontier rather than its traditional signatures.
parsed.market_position: This wine lives on sommelier-driven restaurant lists where adventurous diners seek something different from the California-C Bordeaux paradigm. Retail placement skews toward specialty importers (Jenny & François, Rosenthal) rather than mainstream chains. The collector audience is smaller than Rioja's but growing — Comando G has a 6-to-8-month allocation lag on recent vintages, which tells you demand outpaces supply. Casual drinkers should note: this wine rewards patience and food context; it's not a easy-drinking crowd-pleaser.
parsed.insider_take: Most buyers treat El Reventón as a Garnacha showcase, but the real story is Alicante Henri Bouschet — it's the structural skeleton holding the wine together, adding tannins that let it age like a Cabernet without the varietal cliché. If you dismiss it as a blending grape, you're missing why this wine outlasts most Spanish reds at 10 years old. The table-wine designation trips up collectors who equate appellation status with quality, but Comando G chose this category deliberately to avoid appellation restrictions on blending — the wine is better for it.
